¶
'''thencefrom''' (ᴛ̵ʜens′from′), ''adv.'' [< ''thence'' + ''from.''] From that place. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''thenne<sup>1</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' An old spelling of ''then.''

'''thenne<sup>2</sup>†''', ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thenne'', ''thanne'', ''thonne'', ''theonne'', earlier ''thanene'', ''thanen'', ''theonene'', < AS. ''thanon'', ''theonen'', ''thonon'' (= OHG. ''dannana'', ''dannan'', ''danan'', MHG. G. ''dannen''), thence; with formative ''-nan'', ''-non'', < *''tha'', the pronominal base of ''that'', ''this'', etc., ''then'', ''than'', etc. Hence ''thence.''] From that place; thence.

{{smaller block|Lat men shette the dores and go ''thenne'',
Yet wol the fyr as faire lye and brenne
As twenty thousand men myghte it biholde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath's Tale, l. 285.}}}}

'''thennesforth†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''thenceforth''. ''Chaucer.''

'''thentofore†''', ''adv.'' [< ''then'' + ''tofore''; cf. ''heretofore.''] Before then.

{{smaller block|Bishop Atterbury had ''thentofore'' written largely.
{{right|''Disney'', quoted in N. and Q., 6th ser., X. 147.}}}}

'''Theobroma''' (thē-ō-brō′mä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1737), < Gr. θεός, god (see ''theism''), + βρῶμα, food: see ''broma.''] 1. A genus of trees, of the order ''Sterculiaceæ'' and tribe ''Büttnerieæ''. {{smaller|It is characterized by flowers with inflexed petals each with a spatulate lamina, and anthers two or three in a place between the staminodes or lobes of an urn-shaped stamen-column. The 15 species are natives of the warmer parts of America. They are trees with large oblong undivided leaves, and small lateral solitary or clustered flowers. For ''T. Cacao'', the principal species, see ''cacao'' and ''chocolate''.}}

2. [''l. c.''] A plant of this genus.—'''Oil of theobroma.''' {{smaller|See ''oil''.}}

'''theobromic''' (thē-ō-brō′mik), ''a.'' Derived from ''Theobroma Cacao'': as, ''theobromic'' acid.

¶

'''theocrasy''' (thē-ok′rā-si), ''n.'' [< Gr. θεός, god, + κρᾶσις, a mixing or blending: see ''crasis''.] 1. In ''anc. philos.'', the intimate union of the soul with God in contemplation, which was considered attainable by the newer Platonists. Similar ideas are entertained by the philosophers of India, and by many religious sects.—2. A mixture of the worship of different gods.

'''theocrat''' (thē′ọ-krat), ''n.'' [= F. ''théocrate''; < ''theocrat-ic'': cf. ''democrat'', etc.] A member of a theocracy; one who rules in a theocracy.

'''theocratic''' (thē-ọ-krat′ik), ''a.'' [= F. ''théocratique'' = Sp. ''teocrático'' = Pg. ''theocratico'' = It. ''teocratico'', < NL. *''theocraticus'', < *''theocratia'', theocracy: see ''theocracy''.] Of, pertaining to, or of the nature of a theocracy.

{{smaller block|And the elder Saints and Sages laid their pious framework right
By a ''theocratic'' instinct covered from the people's sight.
{{right|''Lowell'', Anti-Apis.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Kingdom of God existed at the outset in a national form, in the form of a ''theocratic'' state.
{{right|''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 7.}}}}

'''theocratical''' (thē-ọ-krat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''theocratic'' + ''-al''.] Same as ''theocratic''. ''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 124.

'''theocratist''' (thē-ok′ra-tist), ''n.'' [< ''theocrat'' + ''-ist''.] One who emphasizes the principle of authority, placing revelation above individual reason, and order above freedom and progress, and explains the origin of society as a direct revelation from God. ''Encyc. Brit.'', III. 286.

'''Theocritean''' (thē-ok-ri-tē′an), ''a.'' [< ''Theocritus'', < Gr. Θεόκριτος, Theocritus (see def.), + ''-e-an''.] Pertaining to or in the manner of Theocritus

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|theme|6272|Theocritean}}</noinclude>5. In ''philol.'', the part of a noun or verb to which inflectional endings are added; stem; base.

{{smaller block|The variable final letters of a noun are its case-endings; the rest is its ''theme''.
{{right|''F. A. March'', Anglo-Saxon Gram., § 60.}}}}

6. In ''music'', same as ''subject''. The term is sometimes extended to a short melody from which a set of variations is developed.—7†. That by which a thing is done; an instrument; a means.

{{smaller block|Nor shall Vanessa be the ''theme''
To manage thy abortive scheme.
{{right|''Swift'', Cadenus and Vanessa.}}}}

8. A division for the purpose of provincial administration under the Byzantine empire. There were twenty-nine themes, twelve in Europe and seventeen in Asia. Also ''thema''.

{{smaller block|The remaining provinces, under the obedience of the emperors, were cast into a new mould; and the jurisdiction of the presidents, the consulars, and the counts was superseded by the institution of the ''themes'' or military governments, which prevailed under the successors of Heraclius.
{{right|''Gibbon'', Decline and Fall, liii.}}}}

9. In ''logic'', same as ''thema'', 3.=''Syn.'' 1. ''Topic, Point'', etc. (see ''subject''), text.

'''themel†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''thimble''.

'''themer†''' (thē′mėr), ''n.'' One who sets or gives out a theme. ''Tarlton's Jests'', p. 28. (''F. Hall.'')

'''Themis''' (thē′mis), ''n.'' [< L. ''Themis'', < Gr. Θέμις, law, justice personified, Themis, the goddess of justice and right, < τιθέναι (√ θε), set, place, dispose: see ''theme''.] 1. A Greek goddess, the personification of law, order, and abstract right; hence, law and justice personified.

{{smaller block|Such thine, in whom}}

{{smaller block|Can't we touch these bubbles ''then''
But they break? {{right|''Browning'', In a Year.}}}}

{{smaller|''Then'' is often used in offering a substitute for a word or statement rejected.}}

{{smaller block|''Fal.'' Good morrow, good wife.
''Quick.'' Not so, an 't please your worship.
''Fal.'' Good maid, ''then''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 35.}}}}

2†. Than. See ''than''.—'''But then''', but on the other hand; but notwithstanding; but in return.

{{smaller block|He is then a giant to an ape; ''but then'' is an ape a doctor to such a man.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1. 205.}}}}

=''Syn.'' 1. ''Wherefore, Accordingly'', etc. See ''therefore''.

'''then''' (ᴛ̵ʜen), ''a.'' [An ellipsis for ''then being''.] Then being; being at that time.

{{smaller block|Our ''then'' Ambassador was there.
{{right|''J. D.'' (Arber's Eng. Garner, I. 643).}}}}

{{smaller block|It was the letter of the noble lord upon the floor, and of all the king's ''then'' ministers.
{{right|''Burke'', Amer. Taxation.}}}}

{{smaller block|Of quite another stamp was the ''then'' accountant, John Tipp.
{{right|''Lamb'', South-Sea House.}}}}

'''thenadays''' (ᴛ̵ʜen′a̤-dāz), ''adv.'' In those days; in time past: opposed or correlative to ''nowadays''. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The big, roomy pockets which our mothers wore under their gowns—there were no dresses ''thenadays''.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 154.}}}}

'''thenal''' (thē′na̤l), ''a.'' [< ''then''(''ar'') + ''-al''.] Same as ''thenar''.

'''thenar''' (thē′när), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [NL., < Gr. θέναρ (= OHG. ''tenar'', MHG. ''tener'', also OHG. ''tenra'', MHG. ''tenre''), the flat of the hand.] '''I.''' ''n.'' In ''anat.'' and ''zoöl.'', the palm of the hand or sole of the foot; the ball of the thumb; the vola.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the thenar.—'''Thenar muscles''', those muscles which form the fleshy {{smaller block|Our British ''Themis'' gloried with just cause,
Immortal Hale. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii. 257.}}}}

2. The twenty-fourth planetoid, discovered by De Gasparis at Naples in 1853.

'''Themistian''' (thē-mis′ti-an), ''n.'' [< LL. ''Themistius'', founder of the sect, + ''-ian''.] One of a body of Christians also called the Agnoëtæ. See ''Agnoëtæ'', 2.

'''themselves''' (ᴛ̵ʜem-selvz′), ''pron.'', pl. of ''himself'', ''herself'', ''itself'', and used like these words. [< ''them'' + ''selves'', pl. of ''self''.] See ''himself''.

'''then''' (ᴛ̵ʜen), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [Early mod. E. also ''thenne''; also ''than'', ''thanne''; < ME. ''then'', ''thenne'', ''thene'', ''than'', ''thanne'', < AS. ''thænne'', ''thanne'', ''thonne'', then, rel. when, after comparatives than; = OS. ''thanna'' = OFries. ''thenne'', ''thanne'' = D. ''dan'' = OHG. MHG. ''danne'', G. ''dann'', also OHG. ''danna'' MHG. ''denne'', G. ''denn'' = Goth. ''than'', then: see ''than''.] I. ''adv.'' 1. At that time: referring to a time specified, either past or future.

{{smaller block|Ich for-ȝat ȝouthe, and ȝorn in-to elde.
''Thenne'' was Fortune my foo for al here fayre by-heste.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xiii. 14.}}}}

{{smaller block|Now I know in part; but ''then'' shall I know even as also I am known. {{right|1 Cor. xiii. 12.}}}}

{{smaller block|When thou canst get the ring upon my finger, . . . ''then'' call me husband; but in such a "then" I write a "never."
{{right|''Shak.'', All's Well, iii. 2. 62.}}}}

2. Afterward; next in order; soon afterward or immediately.

{{smaller block|First be reconciled to thy brother, and ''then'' come and offer thy gift. {{right|Mat. v. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|First the blade, ''then'' the ear, after that the full corn in the ear. {{right|Mark iv. 28.}}}}

{{smaller block|Their ranks began}}

mass of the ball of the thumb, acting upon the metacarpal and basal phalangeal bone of the thumb, as distinguished from the ''hypothenar muscles'', which similarly act upon the metacarpal bone and first phalanx of the little finger. See ''hypothenar'' and ''thumb''.—'''Thenar prominence''' or '''eminence''', the ball of the thumb.

'''thenardite''' (thē-när′dīt), ''n.'' [Named after L. J. de ''Thénard'' (1777–1857), a French chemist and peer of France.] Anhydrous sodium sulphate (Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>). {{smaller|It occurs in crystalline coatings at the bottom of some lakes at Espartinas (near Madrid), in South America, and in extensive deposits in Arizona. It is used in the preparation of sodium carbonate.}}

'''Thenard's blue.''' Same as ''cobalt blue'' (which see, under ''blue'').

'''thence''' (ᴛ̵ʜens), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thens'', ''thense'', ''thennes'', ''thennus'', ''thannes''; with adv. gen. ''-es'' (see ''-ce''<sup>1</sup>), < ''thenne'', thence: see ''thenne''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''hence'', ''whence''.] 1. From that place.

{{smaller block|Also a lityll ''thense'' ys the place wher ower Savyor Crist taught hys Discipulis to pray.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 29.}}}}

{{smaller block|When ye depart ''thence'', shake off the dust under your feet. {{right|Mark vi. 11.}}}}

2. From that time; after that.

{{smaller block|There shall be no more ''thence'' an infant of days.
{{right|Isa. lxv. 20.}}}}

3. From that source; from or out of this or that; for that reason.

{{smaller block|''Thence'' comes it that my name receives a brand,
And almost ''thence'' my nature is subdued
To what it works in, like the dyer's hand.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxi.}}}}

{{smaller block|Their parents, guardians, tutors, cannot agree; ''thence'' all is dashed, the match is unequal.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 550.}} To break upon the galled shore, and ''than''
Retire again.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1440.}}}}

3. At another time: as, now and ''then'', at one time and another.

{{smaller block|Sometime the flood prevails, and ''then'' the wind;
Now one the better, ''then'' another best.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 5. 10.}}}}

{{smaller block|Now shaves with level wing the deep, ''then'' soars
Up to the fiery concave towering high.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 634.}}}}

'''By then.''' (''a'') By that time: as, Return at four, I shall be ready ''by then.''

{{smaller block|All will be ended ''by then.''
{{right|''Swift'', To Mrs. Johnson, Feb. 23, 1711-12. (''Jodrell.'')}}}}

(''b''†) By the time when or that: ''then'' in this phrase having the force of a relative.

{{smaller block|This evening late, ''by then'' the chewing flocks
Had ta'en their supper on the savoury herb, . . .
I sat me down to watch.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 540.}}}}

'''Every now and then.''' See ''every''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Now and then.''' See ''now''.—'''Till then,''' until that time.

{{smaller block|''Till then'' who knew
The force of those dire arms?
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 93.}}}}

II. ''conj.'' 1. In that case; in consequence; therefore; for this reason.

{{smaller block|So ''then'' they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.
{{right|Gal. iii. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|If God be true, ''then'' is his word true.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 245.}}}}

{{smaller block|He calls the conscience Gods sovrantie; why ''then'' doth he contest with God about that supreme title?
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xv.}}}}

{{smaller block|Not to sit idle with so great a gift
Useless, and ''thence'' ridiculous, about him.
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1501.}}}}

4. Not there; elsewhere; absent.

{{smaller block|They prosper best of all when I am ''thence.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 5. 18.}}}}

'''From thence, fro thence†,''' thence: a pleonasm.

{{smaller block|Aftre gon Men be Watre . . . to Cypre, and so to Athens, and ''fro thens'' to Costantynoble. ''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 55.}}

{{smaller block|All mist ''from thence''
Purge and disperse.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 53.}}}}

{{smaller block|Those who were mounting were dashed upon the rocks, and ''from thence'' tumbled upon the plain.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 54.}}}}

'''thenceforth''' (ᴛ̵ʜens′fôrth′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thennesforth''; < ''thence'' + ''forth''<sup>1</sup>.] From that time forward.

{{smaller block|If the salt have lost his savour, . . . it is ''thenceforth'' good for nothing.
{{right|Mat. v. 13.}}}}

'''From thenceforth,''' thenceforth: a pleonasm.

{{smaller block|And ''from thenceforth'' Pilate sought to release him.
{{right|John xix. 12.}}}}

{{smaller block|Resolving ''from thenceforth''
To leave them to their own polluted ways.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 109.}}}}

'''thenceforward''' (ᴛ̵ʜens′fôr′wärd), ''adv.'' [< ''thence'' + ''forward''<sup>1</sup>.] From that time or place onward.

{{smaller block|''Thenceforward'' oft from out a despot dream
The father panting woke.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer's Field.}}}}

'''thencefrom''' (ᴛ̵ʜens′from′), ''adv.'' [< ''thence'' + ''from.''] From that place. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''thenne<sup>1</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' An old spelling of ''then.''

'''thenne<sup>2</sup>†''', ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thenne'', ''thanne'', ''thonne'', ''theonne'', earlier ''thanene'', ''thanen'', ''theonene'', < AS. ''thanon'', ''theonen'', ''thonon'' (= OHG. ''dannana'', ''dannan'', ''danan'', MHG. G. ''dannen''), thence; with formative ''-nan'', ''-non'', < *''tha'', the pronominal base of ''that'', ''this'', etc., ''then'', ''than'', etc. Hence ''thence.''] From that place; thence.

{{smaller block|Lat men shette the dores and go ''thenne'',
Yet wol the fyr as faire lye and brenne
As twenty thousand men myghte it biholde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath's Tale, l. 285.}}}}

'''thennesforth†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''thenceforth''. ''Chaucer.''

'''thentofore†''', ''adv.'' [< ''then'' + ''tofore''; cf. ''heretofore.''] Before then.

{{smaller block|Bishop Atterbury had ''thentofore'' written largely.
{{right|''Disney'', quoted in N. and Q., 6th ser., X. 147.}}}}

'''Theobroma''' (thē-ō-brō′mä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1737), < Gr. θεός, god (see ''theism''), + βρῶμα, food: see ''broma.''] 1. A genus of trees, of the order ''Sterculiaceæ'' and tribe ''Büttnerieæ''. {{smaller|It is characterized by flowers with inflexed petals each with a spatulate lamina, and anthers two or three in a place between the staminodes or lobes of an urn-shaped stamen-column. The 15 species are natives of the warmer parts of America. They are trees with large oblong undivided leaves, and small lateral solitary or clustered flowers. For ''T. Cacao'', the principal species, see ''cacao'' and ''chocolate''.}}

2. [''l. c.''] A plant of this genus.—'''Oil of theobroma.''' {{smaller|See ''oil''.}}

'''theobromic''' (thē-ō-brō′mik), ''a.'' Derived from ''Theobroma Cacao'': as, ''theobromic'' acid.

'''theobromine''' (thē-ọ̄-brō′min), ''n.'' [< ''Theobroma'' + ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] A crystalline alkaloid (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>N<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>), forming salts with acids, volatile and very bitter. {{smaller|In composition it is nearly related to thein or caffein. It is found in the seeds of ''Theobroma Cacao.''}}

'''theochristic''' (thē-ọ̄-kris′tik), ''a.'' [< Gr. θεόχριστος, anointed by God (< θεός, god, + χριστός, anointed: see ''Christ''), + ''-ic.''] Anointed by God. [Rare.]

'''theocracy''' (thē-ok′ra̤-si), ''n.''; pl. ''theocracies'' (-siz). [= F. ''théocratie'' = ''teocracía'' = Pg. ''theocracia'' = It. ''teocrazia,'' < NL. *''theocratia,'' < Gr. θεοκρατία, the rule of God, < θεός, god, + -κρατία, < κρατεῖν, rule.] 1. A form of government in which God is recognized as the supreme civil ruler of the state, and his laws are taken as the statute-book of the kingdom.—2. A state so governed: usually applied, with the definite article, to the Jewish commonwealth from the time of its organization under Moses until the inauguration of the monarchy under Saul.

{{smaller block|Thus, the Almighty becoming their king, in as real a sense as he was their God, the republic of the Israelites was properly a ''Theocracy.''
{{right|''Warburton,'' Divine Legation, v. 2.}}}}

'''theocrasy''' (thē-ok′rā-si), ''n.'' [< Gr. θεός, god, + κρᾶσις, a mixing or blending: see ''crasis''.] 1. In ''anc. philos.'', the intimate union of the soul with God in contemplation, which was considered attainable by the newer Platonists. Similar ideas are entertained by the philosophers of India, and by many religious sects.—2. A mixture of the worship of different gods.

'''theocrat''' (thē′ọ-krat), ''n.'' [= F. ''théocrate''; < ''theocrat-ic'': cf. ''democrat'', etc.] A member of a theocracy; one who rules in a theocracy.

'''theocratic''' (thē-ọ-krat′ik), ''a.'' [= F. ''théocratique'' = Sp. ''teocrático'' = Pg. ''theocratico'' = It. ''teocratico'', < NL. *''theocraticus'', < *''theocratia'', theocracy: see ''theocracy''.] Of, pertaining to, or of the nature of a theocracy.

{{smaller block|And the elder Saints and Sages laid their pious framework right
By a ''theocratic'' instinct covered from the people's sight.
{{right|''Lowell'', Anti-Apis.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Kingdom of God existed at the outset in a national form, in the form of a ''theocratic'' state.
{{right|''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 7.}}}}

'''theocratical''' (thē-ọ-krat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''theocratic'' + ''-al''.] Same as ''theocratic''. ''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 124.

'''theocratist''' (thē-ok′ra-tist), ''n.'' [< ''theocrat'' + ''-ist''.] One who emphasizes the principle of authority, placing revelation above individual reason, and order above freedom and progress, and explains the origin of society as a direct revelation from God. ''Encyc. Brit.'', III. 286.

'''Theocritean''' (thē-ok-ri-tē′an), ''a.'' [< ''Theocritus'', < Gr. Θεόκριτος, Theocritus (see def.), + ''-e-an''.] Pertaining to or in the manner of Theocritus of Sicily (third century {{sc|b. c.}}), the founder of the Greek idyllic school of poetry; pastoral; idyllic.

{{smaller block|In England the movement in favor of ''Theocritean'' simplicity which had been introduced by Spenser in the Shepherd's Calendar was immediately defeated by the success of Sir Philip Sidney's Arcadia.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVIII. 346.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
